newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels flex muscles before talks, take town.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels flex muscles before talks, take town.

text.p: Zairean rebels flexed their muscles on Friday before planned talks with President Mobutu Sese Seko's shaky government, grabbing another town in mineral-rich Shaba province.

The capture of Kasenga reinforced their supremacy in the field in the run-up to talks in South Africa where the rebels say the issue will not be whether the ailing Mobutu transfers power but how and when.
"I think rebel strategy centres around talking while fighting and fighting while talking," a regional military source told Reuters in Nairobi.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila controls about a quarter of Zaire, five months after starting the revolt in the east, and his supporters already call him "president".

On Thursday Kabila and Mobutu aides agreed at an African summit in Togo to hold their first negotiations in the next few days. Both sides accepted the principles of a ceasefire and negotiations, a summit statement said.

There were strong signals the talks will be in South Africa early next week but the rebels have clearly laid down their agenda: no prior ceasefire and the negotiations must be about ending Mobutu's 32-year-reign in the vast country.

Moise Nyarugabo, secretary-general at rebel headquarters in the eastern city of Goma, told Reuters the issue on the table was the transfer of power from the ailing Mobutu to a transitional government led by Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL).
"The principle is the alliance would form the government, it is not a question of power-sharing. Mobutu's party has been in power for 30 years and the results are evident," he said.
As he spoke, the alliance's disciplined fighters were capturing Kasenga, 220 km (135 miles) north of the Shaba provincial capital and Zaire's second city, Lubumbashi.
"It is definitely rebel troops who are in control of Kasenga," an expatriate source with contacts in Kasenga told Reuters in Lubumbashi.
He and other sources, who declined to be identified, said it was a lightning takeover and by midday the town of about 17,000 people on the Luapula river bordering Zambia was quiet.
One foreign source said some people with gunshot wounds turned up in Kasenga hospital seeking treatment on Friday.
They were civilians injured by retreating soldiers of Mobutu's demoralised army, the FAZ.

Shaba sits on some of the world's biggest deposits of copper, cobalt and precious metals. Kabila's officials are already meeting foreign mining companies about future concessions, industry sources say.
There was no immediate confirmation of the fall from the government side, in Lubumbashi or Zaire's capital Kinshasa.
The rebels say their other immediate target is Zaire's diamond capital, Mbuji-Mayi.
South African President Nelson Mandela, in India, implicitly confirmed reports that the talks between the warring parties will be held in his country with U.N. blessing.
In Johannesburg, a government source said the foreign ministry was preparing to host negotiations, likely to take place on Monday or Tuesday.

Mobutu took power in 1965 with Western backing and his regime degenerated into wholesale corruption, coining the term "kleptocracy". He returned home a week ago, weakened by fresh cancer treatment in Europe.
In rebel-held Kisangani, aid workers said more than 75,000 exhausted, hungry and sick refugees were scattered around an 82-km (50-mile) stretch of railway line to the south.
Paul Stromberg, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said the Hutu refugees were found on Thursday by aid workers aboard a train carrying food south of the city.

"(At Kasea) I saw the most emaciated people I've ever seen in my life," said a representative of Refugees International on the train. "Many of these people won't last another day without urgent medical attention."
The tens of thousands of Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees are the remnants of 170,000 who fled Tingi Tingi and Amisi this month and have been trekking ever deeper into eastern Zaire.
